extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate (and beginning graduate) mathematics students writing proofs (Math 441 Topology course audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Conventions and standards for composing readable, precise mathematical proofs and exposition (paragraph style, notation, justification, and presentation) aimed at students writing homework and course proofs. Emphasizes audience awareness, level of detail, grammatical usage of symbols, and formal vs informal parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write in paragraph form
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical proofs should be written as ordinary prose in complete sentences organized into paragraphs rather than as terse symbolic sequences or two-column proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although you may construct the argument as terse symbolic steps, the write-up must be in paragraph-style prose because it's easier for human readers to comprehend. Paragraph-style proofs are preferred over symbolic-only presentations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proper English
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow standard conventions of grammar, usage, punctuation, and spelling in mathematical writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use complete sentences, correct punctuation (including a period at the end of every sentence), avoid run-on sentences, maintain subject-verb agreement and parallel structure, and use correct capitalization and spelling. Non-native speakers are advised to have a native speaker review early proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify your audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Write proofs with awareness of who the reader is and what background they have.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the course, assume the reader is a fellow student who knows the same background material but not the specific proof. Tailor level of explanation accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include the right amount of detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide how much detail to include based on your own work-through and what would be obvious to the intended reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an argument feels tedious to work through, do it fully first so you know it works; omit details only if they would be obvious to the audience. Include enough to give the reader the 'Aha!' experience and to make clear to the grader that you understood the details. Judging detail is subtle and requires practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label your theorems clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly label each result you prove (Theorem, Proposition, Lemma, Corollary) and state it precisely in English sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You need not copy problem statements verbatim, but indicate the label (e.g., underline 'Theorem' in handwritten work). Choose labels to signal role: Proposition (interesting but not main), Lemma (useful intermediate result), Corollary (follows easily from a theorem). In typeset work, 'Theorem' often in bold and statement italicized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show where proofs begin and end
rubrics_metrics.description: Each proof should explicitly begin with the word 'Proof' and end with a QED marker (e.g., 'QED' or a square symbol).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visibly marking the start and end of a proof helps readers locate and parse arguments; use conventional markers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write with precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Every mathematical statement must have a precise meaning and terms must be used correctly according to their definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vague or intuitive statements inside the formal proof; any informal remarks should be clearly labeled as not part of the formal proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define your terms and variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Give precise definitions for any term or symbol the audience might not know and assign precise meaning to every symbolic variable before first use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ways to give meaning to a variable include: (1) quantifying it (e.g., 'For every x ∈ R,...'), (2) assuming it is an arbitrary element ('Let x ∈ R'), or (3) defining it by an equation or assignment ('Let x = y+z' or 'Let x be the unique positive number such that x^2 = y'). If using an equation to define a variable, put the variable being defined on the left-hand side. Use words like 'set' or 'define' as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify every step
rubrics_metrics.description: Each step in a proof must be justified by an accepted source of justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valid justifications include: definition, axiom, previous theorem, hypothesis, a previous step in the same proof, or rules of logic. When beginning, explicitly state the justification for each step; with practice, obvious justifications may be omitted, but always be conscious of why each step holds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask the two key questions for each sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: For every sentence in your proof be able to answer: what does it mean, and why is it true?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these questions as a check on clarity and validity of each assertion you write.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write clearly (use informal explanations where helpful)
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to formal precision, ensure the exposition is clear and comprehensible; provide intuitive explanations and roadmaps for longer arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For arguments longer than a few sentences, begin by describing informally the plan, execute it, and then summarize what was done. If the proof style is nonstandard (contrapositive, contradiction, induction, etc.), state it up front: e.g., 'We will prove the contrapositive' or 'We will prove this by contradiction.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersperse formulas with explanatory text
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not present long runs of symbolic formulas without words; intersperse equations with explanatory sentences stating what is being done and why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long sequences of equations can be precise yet incomprehensible; include short prose to indicate why steps follow and what the formulas represent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish formal vs informal parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Make it easy for the reader to tell which parts of the paper/proof are formal (definitions and logical steps) and which are informal (motivation, intuition, sketches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label informal discussion as such; keep the formal proof separate and clearly identified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use first person singular sparingly; prefer 'we'
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using 'I' in mathematical exposition; use 'we' when it reasonably refers to the writer and reader together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'we' for statements like 'We will prove the theorem by induction.' If you truly mean only yourself, it's acceptable to use 'I' (e.g., 'I learned this technique...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid most abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use informal abbreviations (e.g., 'iff', 's.t.', 'w.r.t.') in written exposition; prefer full words or standard formal abbreviations only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abbreviations common on the board or in notes are inappropriate for formal written exposition. Exceptions: standard formal abbreviations like 'i.e.' and 'e.g.' may be used but be sure you know their meanings and differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofread
rubrics_metrics.description: Read your proofs end-to-end after writing to catch mistakes and improve clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofreading often uncovers many avoidable errors; do it before submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use symbols and formulas appropriately (they aid clarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical symbols and formulas are useful and often make writing clearer when used judiciously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer symbolic notation when it makes expressions clearer (e.g., 'The area is 1/2 bh' vs a long English phrase), but avoid excessive symbol use that creates obscure prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid logical symbols in English sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not replace words like 'for all' or 'there exists' with logical symbols such as ∃ or ∀ in ordinary exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logical symbols belong in symbolic logic formulas; in ordinary mathematical writing, write the words. Exceptions: ⇒ and ⇔ may be used to connect symbolic statements; in logic-heavy texts the use of logical symbols is different.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place small symbols inline; display large/important formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Include single symbols and short formulas inline with text; center large or important formulas on their own line (displayed formula).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Displayed formulas should be used for emphasis or readability. If a displayed formula ends a sentence it must be followed by a period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure every formula has a grammatical function
rubrics_metrics.description: Every symbol or formula must serve a definite grammatical role in a sentence (typically as a noun expression or a clause).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulas usually function either as expressions acting like nouns or as complete clauses (statements). Read sentences aloud to check grammatical function; many symbols can be read in several ways depending on context ('=' can be read 'equals', 'is equal to', etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use relation/operator symbols only to connect symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols for relations (e.g., =, ∈, ⊂) and operators (+, −, ∩) should connect mathematical symbols, not mix words and symbols directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrong: 'If x is a real number that is > 2, then...' Right: 'If x is a real number and x > 2, then...'. Keep words and symbols properly separated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format complicated fractional expressions carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Inline fractions that are complicated should be displayed; use slash notation for inline fractions that fit a line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write inline fractions as x/(y+2) rather than a stacked fraction. Use displayed horizontal-bar fractions only when necessary; small numerical fractions like 1/2 may be included inline if sized appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid beginning a sentence with a symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not start a sentence with a mathematical symbol because symbols cannot be capitalized to signal sentence start.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reword sentences to place words at the start: e.g., instead of 'f is a continuous function' write 'The function f is continuous.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid placing two formulas separated only by punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not write two consecutive formulas with only a comma between them because they can look like one long formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpose words such as 'then' to separate symbolic statements: wrong: 'If x ≠ 0, x^2 > 0.' Better: 'If x ≠ 0, then x^2 > 0.'
